Renovation Permits feel exciting right up until a project gets delayed by missing permits, strata rules, or inspection issues. If you’re renovating in Vancouver (or nearby cities like Burnaby, North Vancouver, West Vancouver, and Coquitlam), this guide will help you plan the “paperwork” side of your remodel so construction stays smooth.

Why permits matter (even for “simple” renovations)

Renovation permits exist to protect safety, building integrity, and neighbors—especially in multi-unit buildings. If you skip required permits, you can face stop-work orders, insurance complications, resale headaches, and expensive rework.

Quick checklist: do you likely need a permit?

In Vancouver, you typically need permits when your renovation includes any of the following:

  • Moving or removing interior walls (especially if structural)
  • Moving or installing plumbing, electrical, or gas lines
  • Structural repairs or changes
  • Work affecting fire separations in multi-unit buildings (condos/townhomes)
  • Creating new space (finishing an attic/basement, additions, etc.)

The City of Vancouver lists “moving interior walls” and changes to plumbing/electrical/gas lines as common examples that require a permit.

Common renovation projects (and what usually triggers permits)

Kitchen renovations

Cosmetic updates (cabinets, counters, flooring, paint) often don’t require a building permit. But once you move plumbing, gas, electrical, or walls, permits are commonly required.

Bathroom remodels

Swapping finishes is usually straightforward. Relocating fixtures, adding ventilation, or changing plumbing lines is where permits and inspections become important.

Basement finishing and legal suites

Basements are one of the most regulated upgrades because they can affect egress, smoke/fire separation, and mechanical systems. If you’re planning a legal suite, approvals become even more important.

Removing a wall (open concept layouts)

If there’s any chance a wall is load-bearing, you’ll want an engineer’s review and a proper permit path. Done right, this is one of the best “daily life” upgrades; but it must be safe and compliant.

Condo renovations (strata reality check)

Condo work often needs two green lights:

  1. Strata approval (rules around noise hours, elevator booking, debris removal, insurance requirements, and approved contractors)
  2. City permits (plus trade permits) if you’re changing walls, plumbing, electrical, ventilation, or fire separation

Tip: Get strata bylaws and “renovation permits package” documents early; this alone can save weeks.

Don’t forget trade permits: electrical (and sometimes more)

Even when a building permit is in progress, you may still need separate trade permits depending on the work. Technical Safety BC describes homeowner electrical permits and examples like moving outlets/switches or connecting permanently installed equipment. In practice, most homeowners prefer hiring licensed professionals for electrical and gas work, faster approvals, safer installs, and cleaner inspections.

A realistic permit timeline (what most homeowners underestimate)

  • Planning & design: final layout, material choices, scope clarity
  • Drawings & documents: enough detail for reviewers/inspectors
  • Permit review time: varies by project complexity and the city
  • Trade permits + inspections: scheduled at key stages (rough-in, final, etc.)

The best way to avoid delays is to finalize the scope before you apply. Mid-project changes often trigger re-submissions and new inspections.

Budget tip: plan for “hidden” permit-related costs

  • Drawing/engineering fees (especially for structural changes)
  • Upgrades required to meet code (venting, fire separation, safety items)
  • Inspection scheduling and coordination
  • Strata deposits or move-in/out elevator bookings (condos)

A clear scope and a contractor who manages permits and inspections can prevent the most expensive surprises.

We can guide you through planning, permit coordination, and build execution; so your renovation stays compliant and on schedule.

FAQ

Do I need a permit to renovate my kitchen in Vancouver?

If it’s cosmetic (new cabinets, counters, flooring), often no. If you move walls or change plumbing/electrical/gas lines, you typically need permits.

Do I need a permit to remove an interior wall?

If a wall is structural or you’re reconfiguring partitions in a way that affects safety or systems, permits are commonly required. When in doubt, confirm before demolition.

What’s the difference between strata approval and a city permit?

Strata approval is permission from your building (rules, scheduling, contractor requirements). A city permit is legal approval to do regulated construction work. Many condo projects need both.

Renovating a home is an exciting step, but it also comes with many questions about cost, timelines, design choices, and project planning. Many homeowners in Vancouver and the Lower Mainland want to upgrade their living space, but they are unsure where to start or what to expect during the renovation process.

In this blog, we answer some of the most common home renovation questions homeowners ask before beginning their project — so you can make informed, confident decisions about your home.

What Should I Do First Before Starting a Home Renovation?

The first step is always defining your goals. Ask yourself what you want to improve — functionality, layout, aesthetics, or property value. Once the vision is clear, the next step is planning the budget and determining which areas of the home should be prioritized. A well-organized plan helps prevent unexpected costs and delays later in the project.

How Long Does a Typical Home Renovation Take?

Renovation timelines vary based on project size and complexity. A small cosmetic update may take a few weeks, while full home remodeling can take several months. Scheduling, material availability, and design changes can also influence the overall duration. Clear communication and realistic expectations help keep the project on track.

Is It Better to Renovate One Room at a Time or the Whole House?

Both approaches can work, depending on your budget and lifestyle. Renovating room-by-room allows costs to be spread out over time, while full-home renovation creates a more consistent design and may be more efficient overall. Homeowners who plan to modernize layouts, update systems, or increase property value often benefit from doing larger phases together.

How Do I Know Which Renovations Add the Most Value?

Upgrades that improve comfort, functionality, and structural condition typically offer the best long-term value. Kitchens, bathrooms, flooring, and energy-efficient improvements often provide strong returns, especially when combined with timeless design and quality materials.

How Can I Keep My Renovation on Budget?

A realistic budget should include materials, labor, and a contingency amount for unexpected conditions behind walls or floors. Making decisions early, avoiding frequent design changes, and selecting high-quality but practical finishes can help reduce extra costs. Careful planning is the key to staying financially comfortable throughout the project.

Should I Move Out During a Renovation?

For small or partial renovations, many homeowners continue living in the home. However, major remodeling — especially involving kitchens, bathrooms, or structural work — may be more comfortable to manage while temporarily staying elsewhere. Safety, noise, and dust levels should always be considered before deciding.

Frequently Asked Questions About Home Renovation

What is the biggest mistake homeowners make when renovating?

The most common mistake is starting a renovation without a clear plan or defined priorities. This often leads to budget overruns, delays, and design revisions mid-project.

How do I choose the right design style for my renovation?

A good approach is to focus on timeless design first, then incorporate personal style through finishes and details. This helps maintain long-term appeal and functionality.

Is renovating an older home worth it?

Yes — many older homes have strong structure and character. Renovation allows homeowners to modernize layouts, improve comfort, and preserve the home’s long-term value.

These two resources together help you understand both real project costs and local expectations.

How can I prepare my home before the renovation starts?

Remove fragile items, organize belongings, protect personal spaces, and clearly identify areas of work. Good preparation helps create a smoother and safer renovation environment.

Earthquake Threat in Vancouver: What You Need to Know

Vancouver is located in a seismically active region, making earthquakes a constant—though often unnoticed—part of daily life. While most tremors are too small to feel, history has proven that powerful and destructive earthquakes can and do occur. With past earthquakes reaching magnitudes of 7.0 and higher, experts warn that the “Big One” is inevitable. The real question is not if, but when.

Understanding Vancouver’s earthquake risks and how to prepare is crucial for residents, businesses, and city planners.

Act Now to Protect Your Home and Health! 📞 Call Now: +1 604-800-3900

Available 24/7 for immediate assistance!

Vancouver Earthquake History

  • 1946 – A 7.3 magnitude earthquake struck Vancouver Island, causing widespread damage.
  • 1918 – A 7.0 magnitude earthquake occurred in British Columbia, highlighting the region’s vulnerability.

How Often Do Earthquakes Happen in Vancouver?

  • Vancouver experiences small earthquakes daily, but most are too minor to be felt.
  • A damaging earthquake occurs about once every 20 years.

What Are the Chances of a Major Earthquake in Vancouver?

The probability of a large-magnitude earthquake occurring off the West Coast is estimated at 1 in 400 years.

The “Really Big One,” a shallower but highly destructive quake, has an estimated 1 in 25,000-year chance, according to experts.

Are Vancouver High-Rises Earthquake-Proof?

No, Vancouver’s high-rise buildings are not fully earthquake-proof. While modern structures follow seismic safety codes, many older buildings remain at risk of damage or collapse in a major earthquake.

How to Earthquake-Proof Your Home

  • Reinforce the foundation to prevent structural failure.
  • Secure walls, floors, and the roof to withstand lateral and vertical forces.
  • Bolt heavy furniture and appliances to walls to prevent them from falling.
  • Upgrade to earthquake-resistant materials for better durability.

Emergency Preparedness: What You Can Do Today

Create an earthquake emergency kit with water, food, first-aid supplies, and essential medications.

Secure heavy objects to walls to minimize falling hazards.

Develop an evacuation plan for your home or business.

Stay informed by following earthquake alerts and safety recommendations.

How to select a contractor for a project? 

Check references about the quality of their products, their workmanship and their customer service. Inquire about their professional reputation and years in business with the Better Business Bureau. A contractor with more than five years of experience is preferable. Get multiple bids before deciding. 

What should I look for in a contract with a contractor? 

So, what should be in a contractor’s contract? Include whatever is important to you. Drawings are critical. Scope of the work included and not included. Materials to be used. Expected start and completion dates. How long is the pricing valid. How long would you expect the contract to be? Depending on the job. 

What are the types of contracts? 

 How to read a construction contract? 

  1. Scope of work. The first section that you should review is the scope of work described in the contract. 
  2. Contract amount. 
  3. Project schedule. 
  4. Contract documents. 
  5. Dispute resolution method. 
  6. ‘Pay-when-paid’ or ‘pay-if-paid’ 
  7. Termination for convenience. 
  8. No damage for delay. 

How do you evaluate a contractor? 

5 Metrics to Use in Contractor Performance Reviews 

1 – Check-In Compliance. 

2 – Response Time. 

3 – Work Order Completion Percentage. 

4 – First-Time Completion Percentage. 

5 – Location-Based KPIs. 

What are the 4 rules of contract law? 

A law contract is a legally binding agreement between two or more parties with the capacity to agree. For a contract to be valid, it must meet four key essentials: 

offer, acceptance, consideration, and the intent to create legal relations. 

What makes a contract invalid? 

A contract is invalid if any of the following conditions apply: The terms of a contract specify the illegal activity. One of the parties to which the agreement relates doesn’t have legal capacity (it is mentally incapable of entering into a legally binding agreement).
